paragraphs: This custom had a further advantage. Between the two elections, citizens from the country had time to learn about the merits of the candidate provisionally chosen, so they did not have to vote without knowing the case. But under the pretext of speeding things up, the custom was abolished, and both elections were held on the same day.

The _Comitia Tributa_ were properly the council of the Roman people. Only the tribunes could convene them. In them the tribunes were elected and passed their plebiscita. The senate not only had no standing there but no right even to be present. The senators, forced to obey laws they could not vote on, were in this respect less free than the humblest citizens. This injustice was thoroughly ill-conceived, and by itself was enough to invalidate the decrees of a body to which not all its members were admitted. Even if all the patricians had attended the comitia by right as citizens, as mere private individuals they would have had no great influence on a vote counted by heads, where the humblest proletarian was as good as the _princeps senatus_.

So we can see that, besides the order gained by these various ways of distributing so large a people and collecting its votes, the methods were not forms that made no difference in themselves. The results of each depended on the aims for which it was preferred.

Without going into further detail, we can gather from the above that the _Comitia Tributa_ were the most favorable to popular government, and the _Comitia Centuriata_ to aristocracy. The _Comitia Curiata_, in which the populace of Rome was the majority, suited only tyranny and evil designs. They naturally fell into disrepute, and even seditious people avoided a method that revealed their schemes too plainly. It is beyond dispute that the whole majesty of the Roman people lay in the _Comitia Centuriata_ alone, since it alone included everyone: the _Comitia Curiata_ excluded the rural tribes, and the _Comitia Tributa_ excluded the senate and the patricians.

As for the way of taking the vote, among the ancient Romans it was as simple as their morals, though not as simple as at Sparta. Each man declared his vote aloud, and a clerk wrote it down. The majority in each tribe decided the vote of the tribe, the majority of the tribes that of the people, and so with _curiæ_ and centuries. This custom was good as long as honesty prevailed among the citizens and each man was ashamed to vote publicly for an unjust proposal or an unworthy candidate. But when the people grew corrupt and votes were bought, it was fitting for voting to become secret, so that buyers would be held back by mistrust and rogues given a way of not being traitors.

I know that Cicero attacks this change and blames it in part for the ruin of the Republic. I feel the weight Cicero’s authority must carry on such a point, but I cannot agree with him. I hold, on the contrary, that too few changes like this will hasten the destruction of the State. A diet that keeps the healthy well does not suit the sick, and in the same way we should not try to govern a corrupted people with the laws a good people requires. There is no better proof of this rule than the long life of the Republic of Venice, whose shadow still exists, solely because its laws suit only wicked men.

So the citizens were given tablets, which let each man vote without anyone knowing how he voted. New methods were also introduced for collecting the tablets, counting the voices, comparing the numbers, and so on. Yet all these precautions did not stop the good faith of the officers in charge of these tasks[2] from often being suspect. Finally, edicts were issued to prevent intrigues and trafficking in votes, but their very number shows how useless they were.

Toward the close of the Republic, extraordinary expedients were often needed to make up for the inadequacy of the laws. Sometimes miracles were supposed. This could fool the people but not those who governed. Sometimes an assembly was called in a hurry, before the candidates had time to form their factions. Sometimes a whole sitting was filled with talk, when it was seen that the people had been won over and was about to take the wrong side. But in the end ambition got around every attempt to check it. And the most incredible fact of all is that, in the midst of all these abuses, the vast people, thanks to its ancient regulations, never stopped electing magistrates, passing laws, judging cases and carrying on public and private business, almost as easily as the senate itself could have done.
